question: Bronchiolitis predominantly affects infants under 2 years of age, is most commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and is managed supportively — antibiotics, bronchodilators, and corticosteroids are NOT routinely recommended as they do not alter the clinical course.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Bronchiolitis (RSV, infants <2 years) has a purely supportive management — the evidence does NOT support routine use of antibiotics, bronchodilators, or corticosteroids. This is a common exam trap: do not reflexively prescribe salbutamol for wheezing in an infant with typical bronchiolitis features.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Bronchiolitis is the most common severe respiratory illness in infants, peaking in the first year of life, with RSV responsible for 70–80% of cases. Landmark trials (AAP, SIGN, NICE) have confirmed that bronchodilators (salbutamol, ipratropium), corticosteroids, and antibiotics do not improve clinical outcomes. Management is purely supportive: adequate oxygenation (SpO2 ≥94%), careful nasogastric or IV fluid management when feeding is impaired, and monitoring for apnoeas in young infants.
